Each atomic action is annotated as a segment with three fields: a skill category, an action description, and start and end frames (Figure 1, center).

abstract: Fine-grained action annotations can support skill reuse and compositional generalization in robot policies. However, robot datasets typically provide task-level instructions without subtask annotations. Although some include subtask labels, inconsistent formats and conventions hinder cross-source joint training. We propose RoboAtom-Data, which adds unified, time-aligned atomic-action annotations to existing data from multiple sources, covering 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments, and 16,882.1 hours. Our pipeline combines a unified protocol, large-scale manual annotation, propagation across repeated executions with the same ordered skill sequence, and multi-stage quality control. We evaluate the dataset through automatic atomic-action annotation and robot control. We construct RoboAtom-Bench to standardize evaluation of skill recognition and temporal boundary localization. Trained on the annotated data, RoboAtom-Anno achieves better automatic annotation performance than all evaluated open- and closed-source models on both RoboAtom-Bench and the external WGO-Bench. For robot control, atomic-action supervision paired with hierarchical execution improves task success over task-level baselines on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and construction pipeline to support further research on skill-level robot learning.

sections.body: Most robot datasets give only task-level instructions. Existing subtask-annotated sources differ in vocabulary, granularity and temporal coverage. The paper introduces RoboAtom-Data, covering 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million segments and 16,882.1 hours. Manual annotation costs about 100 USD per source-video hour, and GPT-5.6-sol reaches a Skill F1@0.7 of only 21.4 on RoboAtom-Bench. The section lists three contributions: the dataset built with PhysExtend propagation, RoboAtom-Bench, and downstream validation on annotation and robot control.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: RoboAtom-Data adds time-aligned atomic-action labels to 1.45 million trajectories from 16 sources.

sections.body: Related work covers robot datasets, video temporal grounding, and atomic-action supervision. Open X-Embodiment, DROID and RH20T provide scale or sensor diversity. AgiBot World, Galaxea, RoboInter-Data and BEHAVIOR-1K provide subtask annotations, but their vocabularies, granularity and temporal coverage prevent direct pooling. Cortex propagates boundaries from reference segmentations, but variation in speed and pauses can complicate alignment. WGO-Bench identifies temporal localization as a major bottleneck. The section states that cross-source annotation consistency and standalone quality evaluation remain less explored.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior subtask-annotated datasets use inconsistent vocabularies and granularity, and reference-based boundary propagation can struggle with variable execution speed.

sections.body: Each segment holds a skill category, an action description, and start and end frames, and a new segment begins only when the dominant skill changes. Source labels are screened with Qwen3.8-27B and GPT-5.6-sol, with human review for remaining cases. Human seed annotation costs about 100 USD per source-video hour. PhysExtend uses a shared ordered skill sequence to propagate boundaries to other trajectories of the same task, using state-action cues. Quality control samples 20 trajectories per dataset–embodiment group. Episode accuracy is 80.5% when seed sequences are consistent and 57.4% when they are not.
sections.heading: RoboAtom-Data
sections.headline: Seed annotations are propagated to same-task trajectories with PhysExtend and released only after 85% segmentation and 75% episode accuracy.

sections.body: RoboAtom-Bench contains 500 expert-reviewed trajectories with 4,018 ground-truth segments. Its 15 skills cover 99.2% of RoboAtom-Data skill-labeled segments. Subsets are Short (200 trajectories), Medium (100), Long (100) and Multiview (100). Metrics are temporal mIoU and F1, Skill F1 at threshold 0.7, and an Edit score that ignores timestamps. The four reference models predict 1.48–1.70 times the ground-truth segment count on Short, but only 0.51–0.65 times on Long. Inspected Long cases merge successive actions into one segment. The authors attribute part of the weak temporal scores to video descriptions that omit event timing.
sections.heading: RoboAtom-Bench
sections.headline: Reference models recover skill order but miss boundaries: GPT-5.6-sol reaches 63.4 Edit but only 28.0 temporal F1@0.7.

sections.body: RoboAtom-Anno starts from Qwen3.5-9B and goes through robot-domain mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with a reward that combines temporal matching, soft overlap, edit similarity and format. On RoboAtom-Bench, RoboAtom-Anno-9B reaches 30.1 Skill F1@0.7 versus 21.4 for GPT-5.6-sol, at 0.006 versus 4.330 USD per video hour. On WGO-Bench Robot it reaches 48.3 temporal F1@0.7 versus 31.3. For control, atomic-action conditioning with System 2 scheduling on the pi0.5 policy reaches 98.20% on LIBERO-Long, 88.18% overall on LIBERO-Plus and 66.17% average on RoboTwin. The task-level baseline reaches 95.00%, 84.05% and 64.37%.
sections.heading: Learning with Atomic-Action Supervision
sections.headline: RoboAtom-Anno-9B outperforms all evaluated reference models on RoboAtom-Bench, and atomic-action control reaches 98.20% on LIBERO-Long.

sections.body: The limitations section states that the role of atomic-action supervision in large-scale policy pretraining has not yet been verified. Scaling real-robot data collection requires substantial hardware and human effort. Egocentric human video, whose volume far exceeds robot data, has not been included. Human atomic actions are often brief and fragmented, with some lasting less than one second, so their boundaries are hard to localize at the current sampling rate. The authors suggest that adapting the approach to human video may require a coarser definition of atomic actions.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Atomic-action supervision has not been tested in large-scale policy pretraining, and egocentric human video is not yet included.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the problem of missing and inconsistent subtask annotations across heterogeneous robot datasets. RoboAtom-Data unifies action semantics and temporal boundaries through a shared protocol, human annotation, PhysExtend propagation, and multi-stage quality assessment. RoboAtom-Bench provides skill-aware temporal evaluation. Two applications are reported: automatic annotation, where RoboAtom-Anno outperforms the evaluated open- and closed-source models, and robot control, where atomic-action supervision with hierarchical execution improves task success over task-level baselines. The section adds no results beyond those in earlier sections.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion reports that RoboAtom-Anno beats evaluated models on annotation and that atomic supervision improves control over task-level baselines.

sections.body: The appendix gives the collaborative annotation pipeline, including prompts and review rules, and per-source statistics for the 16 sources. It lists the 29-class skill vocabulary and the 15-class closed subset that covers 99.2% of released segments. Source-specific mapping rules are given for AgiBot World, Galaxea Open-World, RH20T and RoboCerebra. It documents robot-domain mid-training data totaling 2,841,942 samples. The cost accounting uses a rate of 0.3880208 USD per GPU hour. Image augmentation controls for the pi0.5 baseline on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin are also reported.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists annotation prompts, per-source statistics, skill vocabulary, source mapping rules, training data, cost accounting, and image augmentation controls.
